title: 34,996 Patients in One Year: Family Circle of Care Put East Texas Health Access on the Starting Line
thumbnailMessage: East Texans ran for care that reaches 34,996 patients
summary: Tyler’s first Family Circle Fun Run capped National Health Center Week by supporting a nonprofit that reports serving 34,996 unduplicated East Texas patients in 2025.
content:
East Texans gathered in downtown Tyler on Saturday, Aug. 8, for a 5K and free children’s dash built around a larger community accomplishment: making medical, dental and mental-health care available to families who can face serious barriers to getting it.

The first Family Circle Fun Run was the closing event of National Health Center Week for Family Circle of Care, a nonprofit community health center serving Tyler, Jacksonville, Athens and nearby communities. Registration materials said proceeds support the center’s mission and that the event was designed to bring families, businesses and community partners together around health and access.

A responsible account of the event must stop short of inventing a finish-line total. RepWatchr found the official schedule and beneficiary, but not a verified final count of runners or dollars raised. Those numbers should be added only when the organizer publishes them. The larger service record is already substantial and current: Family Circle of Care says it provided care to 34,996 unduplicated patients in 2025, a 10% increase over 2024.

That figure means individual patients, not appointments. A patient may have received multiple services during the year, so it should not be multiplied or described as 34,996 visits. The center also reports that its pediatric clinicians saw 19,264 children ages 0 through 18 in 2025 and that it provided prenatal and postpartum care to 1,570 women. Those are the organization’s published figures.

The work is spread across a practical network. Family Circle of Care says it operates seven medical clinics, one dental clinic and a mobile medical clinic, with sites in Tyler, Jacksonville and Athens. Its listed services include pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, family medicine, internal medicine, behavioral health, dental care, eye care and social-service navigation. The clinics sit in communities the organization describes as medically underserved, including rural service areas in Jacksonville and Athens.

The center has operated as the area’s community health center since 2013. It is a federally qualified health center, a designation tied to serving underserved areas or populations, providing comprehensive primary care and meeting federal program requirements. Family Circle of Care says it welcomes patients regardless of ability to pay and offers help navigating Medicaid, CHIP, SNAP, Healthy Texas Women and Health Insurance Marketplace applications.

That administrative help is part of the good being recognized. A medical appointment can fail before a patient sees a clinician if the family cannot understand eligibility rules, replace a document, find a plan or connect to transportation and food support. Certified community health workers at the clinics help residents apply for and manage benefits and connect with agencies that provide housing, clothing and other assistance.

The Aug. 8 event translated that mission into a public, family-friendly morning. The posted schedule opened check-in at 7 a.m., placed the free Kids’ Dash at 7:55 and started the 5K at 8. The event was free to attend; the children’s dash was free, while the 5K carried a registration fee. That structure let families participate even if they were not running the paid race.

The community-good story is not that a race by itself solved East Texas health disparities. It did not. The accomplishment is a network of clinicians, staff, patients, volunteers and supporters building an institution that reached nearly 35,000 people in one year, then inviting the wider community to invest in its next year of work.

Quality matters alongside volume. Family Circle of Care says the Health Resources and Services Administration recognized it as a Health Center Quality Leader in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. HRSA explains that its Community Health Quality Recognition badges are based on health-center performance data and recognize achievements in access, quality, outcomes and health information technology. The center also identifies itself as a Level III Patient-Centered Medical Home recognized by the National Committee for Quality Assurance.

Those credentials should not be treated as a guarantee that every patient has the same experience or that every regional need is met. They are evidence that the organization participates in measured quality systems. Patients should still have clear ways to ask questions, report concerns and see whether services are available at a particular site. Community praise is strongest when it leaves room for accountability.

The 2025 numbers also reveal the scale of the workforce behind the mission. Family Circle of Care says more than 280 employees, contractors and medical residents work across the organization. Its West Gentry clinic serves as an outpatient site for the UT Tyler internal-medicine residency program, connecting patient care with training for physicians who may remain in the region.

A community health center’s value is especially visible in the gaps between conventional systems. Some residents are uninsured. Others have Medicaid or Medicare but struggle to find a local provider accepting new patients. Some need pediatric, prenatal, dental and behavioral-health care in the same family. Others need an early appointment, a mobile clinic or help managing several chronic conditions. No single clinic removes every barrier, but an integrated local network reduces the number of doors a family must open alone.

The run’s focus on wellness also makes sense only if it stays inclusive. Health is not a moral score, and a 5K is not accessible to everyone. A strong community event creates roles for walkers, children, volunteers, sponsors, patients and neighbors with disabilities. The organizer’s decision to make attendance and the Kids’ Dash free helped widen participation, while race fees generated support for services. Future events should continue reporting accessibility arrangements, route safety and where proceeds went.

Donors and participants can ask for four simple receipts. First, publish the final number of registered runners and volunteers. Second, publish gross revenue, direct event costs and the net amount transferred to patient services. Third, identify which program or unrestricted fund received the money. Fourth, report a dated outcome later, such as appointments supported or equipment purchased, without exposing patient identities.

Family Circle of Care can also make its 34,996-patient figure more useful by linking it to an annual report or federal Uniform Data System filing when available. The public benefits from knowing how patient counts are defined, how many visits occurred, which services grew, what share of patients were uninsured and where wait times or workforce shortages remain. Transparency would strengthen—not diminish—the achievement.

East Texas residents who need care should use the organization’s official contact information rather than assume every service is offered at every site. The center lists a main appointment number of 903-535-9041 and publishes location-specific services and hours. Medical emergencies still belong with 911 or an emergency department.

People who want to help have options beyond a race registration. They can donate through the official organization, volunteer when vetted opportunities are posted, share clinic information with families who need it, or train for work in community health. Businesses can sponsor preventive-care events. Patients can contribute feedback that helps services improve. Public officials can examine transportation, workforce and reimbursement barriers that a fundraiser cannot fix.

The most patriotic community stories are grounded in neighbors accepting responsibility for one another while demanding honest results. Saturday’s runners and volunteers supported an organization that can point to clinics, services, quality recognition and a verified annual patient count. That is a concrete record of local good.

The next record should be the event result. Until Family Circle of Care publishes it, RepWatchr will not guess. The verified story is already worth telling: in 2025, a Tyler-based nonprofit says it served 34,996 distinct patients across East Texas, including more than 19,000 children, and in August 2026 the community showed up to help keep that circle of care moving.
